title: The attributes
hookLine: one verse says nothing is like Him, and in the same breath calls Him the Hearer, the Seer

lines: AND HE IS THE HEARER, THE SEER.
cards: One sentence of the Qur'an, in two halves. The first half, in Pickthall's translation: "Naught is as His likeness." Nothing is like Him.
Then, in the same breath: "and He is the Hearer, the Seer." Hearing and seeing are things you do. A child does them.
A cat does them. So the verse that says nothing is like Allah goes straight on to describe Him with words we use for ourselves. That isn't a slip.
It's the whole problem of this part in one line.

teach.h: SIFAT: WHAT HE SAYS OF HIMSELF.
teach.b: Day 232 gave you the most beautiful names; today, how theologians speak of them.

The Arabic word is sifat, attributes: the qualities Allah describes Himself with, knowing, willing, powerful, living, hearing, seeing, speaking. Another verse says: "Allah's are the fairest names. Invoke Him by them."
So Muslims call on Him by what He has said of Himself. But how do you use those words without shrinking Him to our size?

Theologians name two ditches beside the road. One is tashbih, likening: hearing like ours, only bigger, with ears and a place to stand. The other is ta'til, emptying out: deciding the words mean nothing at all.
The road runs between, and each school we've met walks it its own way. The Atharis affirm hearing and seeing as they came, and don't ask how.
The Ash'aris and Maturidis affirm a set of attributes as real and eternal, set out by argument, and explain some other descriptions with care.
The Mu'tazilah, guarding oneness, said Allah knows and hears by His very essence, not by attributes added to Him. And Shia theology has its own careful version of that concern.
Different routes, one shared fence: He is not like His creation.
As theologians put it, He hears, but not with ears. He sees, but not with eyes. The word hearing is true of Him; the picture that comes with it isn't.

how: Muslims call on Allah by His names and attributes, such as as-Sami', the Hearer, and al-Basir, the Seer, while holding with Qur'an 42:11 that nothing is like Him; the schools of theology explain the attributes in different ways.

o: a picture of Allah as a much bigger version of ourselves
the qualities of the prophets that Muslims try to copy
the attributes Allah describes Himself with, like hearing and seeing

s: the verse that says nothing is like Allah also calls Him the Hearer, the Seer
Qur'an 42:11 puts both halves in one sentence.
the Mu'tazilah said Allah's knowledge is an attribute added to Him
they said He knows by His very essence, to guard oneness.
avoiding likening means saying the words mean nothing
theologians call that ta'til, the other ditch.

games.q: the Qur'an calls Allah the Hearer. how do the theologians want you to take it?
o: real hearing, but not with ears, and like nothing in creation.
just a figure of speech that means nothing.
games.why: the verse holds both: nothing is like Him, and He is the Hearer. The schools differ in how they explain it, but all avoid likening Him to creation.

practice: Listen, and loosely count the sounds you can hear, a fan, traffic, your own breath, and notice how few you can hold at once: that's our hearing, limited and needing ears.
Now hold the word the verse uses, the Hearer, without building a picture: hearing without any of those limits, and without our shape.
If you pray, you can call on Him by that name, as-Sami'; if you don't, let the phrase nothing like Him be enough.

wordCard.voice: Sifat. The attributes of Allah: hearing, seeing, knowing, willing and more, affirmed without likening Him to anything. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: attributes, qualities; the singular is sifa.

carryVoice: Your line: nothing like him. Real names, and no picture big enough to hold them. Go gently.
